entries.title: The Pit: why a 50% loss needs +100%
entries.hook: Lose half. Now you must double just to break even.
entries.takeaway: A loss is measured from where you started, but the climb back is measured from what is left. So the climb is always the bigger percentage, and it grows faster the deeper the pit.

entries.title: 35% winners can beat 60% winners
entries.hook: 60% winners vs 35% winners. Guess who's losing.
entries.takeaway: How often you win is only half the math. A 60% win rate with small wins and big losses loses money; a 35% win rate with small losses and big wins makes it. The price of the second one is long losing streaks, so plan for them.
entries.question: Can a 35% win rate beat a 60% win rate?

entries.title: R: the only unit a trader needs
entries.hook: You made $500. Proud? Depends what you risked.
entries.takeaway: R is what you lose if your stop gets hit: (entry − stop) × shares, fixed before you buy. Measure every result with that ruler. A $500 win is +5R on $100 risk and +0.25R on $2,000. Losers should all be −1R; anything bigger means the stop moved or price gapped.

entries.title: Legend 01: Jesse Livermore
entries.hook: Made $1 million in a day. Went bankrupt more than once.
entries.takeaway: Jesse Livermore taught himself to read markets from prices, won big in the 1907 panic and the 1929 crash, and built his method around the pivotal point: wait for a key price to break, add only while the trade works, then sit tight. He lost fortunes by breaking those rules: following a friend's cotton tips, buying more as cotton fell, and putting money into businesses outside trading. His 1940 rules are the lessons those losses paid for.

entries.title: The Seesaw: wider stop, smaller size
entries.hook: Always buy 100 shares? Nice round number.
entries.takeaway: Fix the risk first (say 1% of the account), then let the stop set the size: shares = risk ÷ stop distance, rounded down. A wider stop means fewer shares and the same dollars at risk. Buying the same share count every time lets your stop decide your risk instead.

entries.title: Risk 0.5% vs 2% per trade: 1,000 runs
entries.takeaway: With the same trades, risking 2% of the account per trade instead of 0.5% grew faster but made the typical worst drop about four times deeper (−23% vs −6%), because losing streaks hit everyone. Choose the size whose worst drop you could sit through.
entries.question: Same edge: what changes if you risk 2% instead of 0.5%?

entries.title: The Council: where does your stop go?
entries.hook: Where does your stop go? Five legends, two camps.
entries.takeaway: Five legends answer where the stop goes. One camp uses a fixed percent below the buy (O'Neil: 7 to 8%); the other uses the chart (Darvas: just under the range the stock broke out of; Kovner: where the market shouldn't go if you're right, with smaller size). All agree: decide the exit before buying, keep losses small, and go when it hits.
entries.question: Where does your stop go?

entries.title: Expectancy in 15 seconds
entries.hook: Got an edge? One number answers that.
entries.takeaway: Expectancy is what you make or lose per trade, on average. In R: add up every result and divide by the number of trades. Above zero, you have an edge; below zero, you don't.

entries.title: Failure File: averaging down a loser
entries.hook: Down 28% from its high. Bargain, right?
entries.takeaway: Averaging down means buying more as a stock falls. In Cisco's 2000-2002 fall, a buyer adding $10,000 after every further 20% drop had $50,000 in by March 2001, worth about $17,500 at the 2002 low. Each buy went into a trade already losing. One buy with a stop 8% below it would have cost about $800. Never add to a loser.

entries.title: Legend 02: William O'Neil
entries.hook: He turned $5,000 into $200,000. Then he studied why.
entries.takeaway: William O'Neil turned $5,000 into $200,000 as a young broker, then measured what more than 1,000 big winning stocks had in common and shared that research with everyday investors. His favorite setup was the cup with handle, bought as the price broke above the handle on heavy volume, and he cut every loss at 7 to 8%. His fund's slide taught the last rule: don't grow too fast or own too many small stocks.
